outcome: Status rests on Hull, Ibrahim, Paltrowitz, Ter-Saakov and Wang (arXiv:2503.23661, 31 Mar 2025; DMTCS), which settles stamp-folding counts for specific fixed mountain-valley assignments; Hogan's new A001415 terms are finite instances and do not set the status. [Judged 2026-09-28; the researcher's original outcome follows.] No closed formula or general resolution of map/stamp folding counting was found, but two concrete pieces of progress occurred in the window: (1) Hunter Hogan's 'mapFolding' software computed two new exact terms (a(19), a(20)) of OEIS A001415 ('number of ways of folding a 2 x n strip of stamps'), a case of the map-folding counting problem, extending it beyond the previously known a(18); (2) Hull, Ibrahim, Paltrowitz, Ter-Saakov and Wang (arXiv:2503.23661, first posted 31 Mar 2025) settled a restricted case of the stamp-folding problem — foldings with a fixed mountain-valley crease assignment — giving closed forms for specific MV patterns and new upper/lower bounds for others. Both are genuine, verifiable movement on cases of the stated problem; neither is a resolution of the general open counting problem, and no AI system contributed to either.

ai.basis_quote: Ironically, LLMs can't figure it out either because I guess my idea was novel.

summary: The Wikipedia bullet 'Map folding – various problems in map folding and stamp folding' is a bundle of open counting problems (no known closed-form formula or polynomial-time algorithm for the number of ways to fold an n-stamp strip or an n x n map). Nothing in the window resolves the general problem — the current Wikipedia article on map folding (checked live only to confirm current framing, not as evidence of the window's events) still states no closed-form formula or polynomial-time algorithm is known. Two pieces of genuine, verifiable case-level progress occurred: (a) Hunter Hogan's open-source 'mapFolding' package (github.com/hunterhogan/mapFolding) computed OEIS A001415 a(19) and a(20) (2 x n stamp-strip foldings), credited in the OEIS extension line 'a(19)-a(20) from Hunter Hogan, Mar 21 2025' — this narrows a specific sub-case (the 2×n restriction) of the map-folding counting family by adding exact values, which is analogous to the record-extension caveat in §3.1 but here the sequence itself, not a search bound, is the object being extended, so I read it as `partial` progress on that 2×n case rather than mere record-keeping; the repository explicitly disclaims AI help ('Ironically, LLMs can't figure it out either because I guess my idea was novel'), indicating the author tried consulting an LLM and it was unhelpful, so ai_role is `none`. (b) Hull, Ibrahim, Paltrowitz, Ter-Saakov, and Wang, 'The Stamp Folding Problem From a Mountain-Valley Perspective: Enumerations and Bounds' (arXiv:2503.23661, v1 31 Mar 2025, published in DMTCS), restricts the classical stamp-folding count to foldings with a fixed mountain-valley assignment per crease — a genuine restriction/case per §3.1 — and proves closed forms for specific MV patterns (with a Catalan-number appearance) plus bounds for others; this is traditional pen-and-paper/computer-algebra combinatorics with no stated AI involvement of any kind. The triage's 'Sakai boundary-based counting approach (2026)' lead could not be located or verified anywhere — no author of that name, no matching paper, and no snippet reproducing it appeared in any search I ran; I treat it as unverifiable and do not rely on it. I found no claim, credible or otherwise, of an AI system generating, assisting, or bounding any map-folding or stamp-folding result in this window.
competing_reading: One could argue the Hogan OEIS extension is closer to 'progress' (a record/table extension) than 'partial' (a case settled), per the record-extension caveat in §3.1 — the sequence for the 2×n restriction is being extended value-by-value rather than a new case-class being closed. I classify it as partial because A001415 catalogs a specific well-defined restricted sub-problem (2×n map folding) whose enumeration for n=19,20 is now exactly known, which is a settled case rather than a bound; but if one instead reads the whole A001415 sequence as an unbounded 'how far can we compute' exercise akin to a search-limit extension, `progress` would be the better code.
what_would_settle_it: Whether OEIS regards A001415 as counting a well-posed restricted sub-problem (favoring `partial`) versus an open-ended computational frontier akin to a search bound (favoring `progress`) — this would be clarified by how the sequence's own literature (e.g., any accompanying paper) frames the 2×n case.
